addedLines: - augmentor: Implements a single, sharp, well-defined feature or change in an existing codebase with minimal blast radius, staying strictly in line with the codebase's established conventions. Use when you have ONE clearly-scoped addition or modification and want it done surgically. Give it the full spec plus any context you have already gathered; it will fetch whatever else it needs to understand the code. Do NOT use for broad, vague, or multi-feature work, or for anything that would force it to guess at requirements — it will refuse rather than assume. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)

- bugger: Finds and/or fixes bugs within a defined scope, according to orchestrator/user instructions. Operates in two dimensions. Trigger: either it's told about a specific bug (reproduce → find root cause → address it), or it's asked to scan a part of the code for latent bugs. Action: either propose solutions only (diagnosis + recommended fix, no code changed), or actually implement the fix. The instructions tell it which. When it writes fixes, they are surgical and adhere to the codebase's established standards. Use for debugging and bug-hunting; not for building new features. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- debloater: Reviews a specific piece of code or part of the codebase to remove bloat (dead code, redundancy, needless complexity) and improve logical organization, within a defined scope. Two action modes: IDENTIFY only (report the bloat and improvement opportunities it finds, changing nothing) or CLEAN (actually make the improvements). Under no circumstances does it make changes for their own sake — if nothing genuinely needs changing, it changes nothing and says so. Use for cleanup/tidying/simplification of existing code; not for adding features or fixing bugs. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)

- doccer: Documents code within a defined boundary — e.g. code an augmentor just wrote, a file/module/directory, or whatever the user points it at. Collects the context it needs, then writes documentation that matches the codebase's established documentation standards and/or the user's instructions (user instructions always win). Use when you want existing code documented without touching the code itself. It will NEVER modify code — not even to fix obvious bugs or errors; it only adds or edits documentation. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)

- enforcer: Scans code for (1) security issues and vulnerabilities and (2) violations of the codebase's conventions/standards, within a given scope — a specific file, a directory, or a global scan. Two action modes: REPORT only (surface findings to the user/orchestrator, change nothing) or FIX (apply the corrections surgically, conforming to established standards). Use for security review and convention/compliance enforcement. Not for adding features, general bug-hunting, or cleanup/refactoring for its own sake. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- merge-therapist: Resolves merge (or rebase/cherry-pick) conflicts and reports back a highly concise explanation of what it did. Default posture is the most harmonious resolution possible: preserve the intent and functionality of BOTH sides. If the user/orchestrator gives different instructions (prefer one side, drop something, take a specific shape), it follows those instead. Use when a merge/rebase leaves conflicted files, or when you want an in-progress conflict state untangled and explained. Not for doing the merge strategy planning, feature work, or bug-hunting beyond what conflict resolution requires. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, TodoWrite)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- tester: Verifies that ONE specific, already-implemented feature or issue actually behaves the way it is supposed to. Give it (1) what the feature is and (2) what "working" looks like; it exercises the feature — reading code to orient, running curl/CLI/REPL calls, and writing throwaway ad-hoc tests in its own scratch environment — and reports whether the expected behavior holds, with evidence. It does NOT write unit tests into the repo, does NOT modify the codebase, and does NOT review code quality/conventions. Use to confirm a finished change does what it claims; not for building, fixing, or broad regression testing. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, LSP, WebFetch)

content.text:
SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is the protocol for sending mail. An SMTP server accepts a message from a client and relays it toward the recipient's mail server.

**Roles**
- Submission server: accepts mail from authenticated users (port 587, STARTTLS; 465, implicit TLS).
- Relay/MX server: receives mail from other servers on port 25.
- SMTP does not retrieve mail. IMAP (143/993) and POP3 (110/995) do that.

**Transaction**
`EHLO` → `MAIL FROM` → `RCPT TO` → `DATA` → message body → `.` → `QUIT`. Replies are 3-digit codes: 2xx success, 4xx temporary failure (sender retries), 5xx permanent failure (bounce).

**Delivery path**
Client → submission server → DNS MX lookup for recipient domain → recipient's MX server → recipient's mailbox store.

**Authentication for deliverability**
- SPF: DNS record listing IPs allowed to send for the domain.
- DKIM: cryptographic signature on the message, public key in DNS.
- DMARC: policy stating what to do when SPF/DKIM fail, plus reporting.

Without all three, major providers reject or spam-filter the mail.

**Common software**: Postfix, Exim, OpenSMTPD, Microsoft Exchange. Hosted APIs: Amazon SES, SendGrid, Postmark, Mailgun.

**Practical note**: residential and most cloud IPs have port 25 blocked outbound, and their IP reputation is poor. Self-hosting outbound mail usually means mail lands in spam; use a hosted relay instead.

message.content: what makes up an smtp server?

content.text:
Components of an SMTP server:

**Listener (SMTP daemon)** — binds ports 25 (relay), 587 (submission), 465 (implicit TLS); speaks the SMTP command/reply protocol.

**Session state machine** — tracks `EHLO`/`MAIL FROM`/`RCPT TO`/`DATA` order per connection and returns 2xx/4xx/5xx codes.

**TLS layer** — STARTTLS upgrade or implicit TLS; certificate and cipher config.

**Authentication (SASL)** — validates submitting users (PLAIN/LOGIN over TLS, CRAM-MD5, OAUTH); backed by a user store (passwd file, LDAP, database).

**Access control / policy engine** — decides who may relay, rate limits, RBL/DNSBL lookups, greylisting, recipient-address validation.

**Content filtering hooks** — antivirus and spam scanning (e.g. via Milter or a proxy such as Amavis), plus DKIM signing and SPF/DKIM/DMARC verification.

**Message queue** — spool on disk holding accepted messages, with retry timers and backoff for 4xx failures, and bounce generation on expiry.

**Router / resolver** — classifies each recipient as local or remote; for remote, does DNS MX lookup and picks the next hop.

**Outbound delivery agent** — opens SMTP connections to the next hop, manages concurrency and per-destination limits.

**Local delivery agent** — writes to the local mailbox store (Maildir, mbox, or handoff to an IMAP server like Dovecot).

**Alias/rewrite tables** — aliases, virtual domains, canonical address rewriting, forwarding rules.

**Logging** — per-message log with queue IDs, plus DMARC report generation.

In Postfix these are separate processes (`smtpd`, `cleanup`, `qmgr`, `smtp`, `local`, `trivial-rewrite`); in Exim one binary with configuration sections (`acl`, `routers`, `transports`).

Ambiguous. Which do you mean:

- Where an SMTP server sits in the mail path (network topology)?
- Where a specific server's config/binaries live on disk (e.g. Postfix at `/etc/postfix`)?
- Whether one is running on this machine?
- The SMTP host for a specific account or project?

From the same TCP connection the client opened: source IP = the address the daemon bound to, source port = the listening port (25, 587, or 465). Replies are not a separate connection.

If the host has multiple addresses and the daemon binds `0.0.0.0`, replies leave from the address the kernel selected for that connection — the one the client connected to.

For *outbound* delivery the roles swap: your server is the client, so its source port is ephemeral and its source IP is set by the route (Postfix `smtp_bind_address`), which is the IP that must appear in your SPF record.

message.content: so is the smtp server on your machine, on a server somewhere, what is its relationship to you and your mail client?

content.text:
Both exist, and they are different servers.

Your mail client does not run one. It connects out to a **submission server** operated by your mail provider — a machine somewhere on the internet (e.g. `smtp.gmail.com:587`). The client authenticates with your username and password and hands the message over. That is the whole client-side relationship: one authenticated TCP connection, message handed off, connection closed.

The submission server then does the delivery work: queues the message, looks up the recipient domain's MX record, and connects to the **recipient's MX server** — a different machine, run by the recipient's provider, listening on port 25. That server accepts the message and stores it in the recipient's mailbox.

So the chain is three separate machines:

```
your client  --587-->  your provider's submission server  --25-->  recipient's MX server
```

An SMTP server can run on your own machine — that is what `localhost:25` is on a Linux box with Postfix installed, and it is how `sendmail`/cron mail works. But a normal desktop mail client (Thunderbird, Outlook, Mail.app) does not use it; it goes straight to the remote provider.

They do. SMTP is exactly what the client speaks to the submission server — `EHLO`, `AUTH`, `MAIL FROM`, `RCPT TO`, `DATA`.

The distinction is running versus speaking: the client is an SMTP *client*, not an SMTP *server*. It initiates connections and sends commands; it does not listen on a port or accept mail.

message.content: outline the flow from user writes mail, presses send, to recipient receives.

content.text:
1. Client composes the message (headers + body, MIME-encoded).
2. Client opens TCP to the provider's submission server on 587, does STARTTLS, authenticates with SASL.
3. Client sends `EHLO`, `MAIL FROM`, `RCPT TO` per recipient, `DATA`, message, `.` — server returns `250 queued` and the client is done.
4. Submission server DKIM-signs the message and writes it to its queue.
5. Queue manager splits recipients by domain and does a DNS MX lookup for each domain.
6. Outbound agent connects to the recipient's MX server on 25, STARTTLS, replays `MAIL FROM`/`RCPT TO`/`DATA`.
7. MX server checks SPF, DKIM, DMARC, RBLs, and spam/virus filters; returns 250 (accept), 4xx (sender retries later), or 5xx (sender bounces).
8. MX server's local delivery agent writes the message into the recipient's mailbox store.
9. Recipient's client fetches it over IMAP and shows it in the inbox.

message.content: make it a graph, assuming 1 sender, 5 recipients.

content.text:
Assuming the 5 recipients span 3 domains (2 @a.com, 2 @b.com, 1 @c.com):

```
  Sender's client
        │
        │ SMTP submission :587 (TLS + AUTH)
        │ 1 connection, 1 copy, 5 RCPT TO
        ▼
  Provider's submission server
        │  DKIM-sign → queue
        ▼
  Queue manager  ── groups recipients by domain, MX lookup each
        │
        ├──────────────┬──────────────┐
        │ :25          │ :25          │ :25
        ▼              ▼              ▼
   MX a.com        MX b.com       MX c.com
   2 RCPT TO       2 RCPT TO      1 RCPT TO
        │              │              │
   SPF/DKIM/      SPF/DKIM/      SPF/DKIM/
   DMARC + spam   DMARC + spam   DMARC + spam
        │              │              │
        ├───┬───       ├───┬───       │
        ▼   ▼          ▼   ▼          ▼
      mbox mbox      mbox mbox      mbox
       r1   r2        r3   r4        r5
        │   │          │   │          │
        ▼   ▼          ▼   ▼          ▼
       IMAP fetch by each recipient's client
```

One copy leaves the sender; the queue manager fans out to one SMTP connection per destination domain, and each MX server splits to individual mailboxes.
